newsitem.title: CHINA: China copper scrap curbs seen having small impact.
newsitem.headline: China copper scrap curbs seen having small impact.

text.p: Curbs imposed by China on imports of copper scrap will have little impact on the supply of feed for smelters and refiners, an official of the China National Nonferrous Metals Industry Corp (CNNC) said on Monday.

That conclusion stems from a rise in the concentration of copper contained in scrap imports since Beijing began clamping down on low-grade shipments, said Wang Zhongkui, market director of the CNNC's Techno-Economic Research Institute.

Analysts and market sources have said the curbs, introduced on January 1, are likely to hit smelters largely dependent on secondary copper to bridge the gap between demand and the limited output of China's ageing mines.
"The controls may cut the total amount of copper scrap imported.. but the effect on content will not be big," Wang said at a metals conference in Beijing.

"Imports (of copper scrap) from January to September were about 460,000 tonnes," Wang said. "This is quite a big drop compared with last year -- but most of this year's (scrap) imports contain a lot of copper."
In the past China had imported huge amounts of low-grade scrap which yielded very little, but imports now were largely made up of grade one or two scrap, he said.
As imports decline, domestic scrap supplies are also falling due to a drop in prices.
Total scrap availability on the Chinese market in 1996 would probably reach only 520,000 tonnes, a fall of 38 percent from last year, industry analyst Simon Hunt told the conference.

Scrap importers now need environmental licences, which were not being freely issued, while more stringent import inspections had added to the shipping costs of what had become a significant source of feed for refiners and smelters, he said.

"Scrap imports will continue to suffer from the constraints now being placed on importers... cathode production will be constrained by a generally tight, global blister market and by reduced scrap availability," Hunt said.
He added that this would contribute to an expected rise in imports in copper cathode in future.
"China will become a far larger importer of cathode over the next four years than nearly everyone has been forecasting," he said.
